slides.headline: A desert, a pyramid, and a warning
slides.sub: Vasily Vereshchagin, The Apotheosis of War, 1871

slides.headline: Central Asia, 1871
slides.text: A blazing desert, an empty sky, and in the middle, a strange pyramid. Vasily Vereshchagin painted it in 1871. Now come closer.

slides.headline: It's not stone
slides.text: Those blocks aren't stones. Every one is a human skull, piled high. No bodies, no blood, just skull after skull.

slides.headline: The only life
slides.text: The only living things are crows. Some circle overhead, others have already landed on the pile. They know what war leaves behind.

slides.headline: Nothing grows here
slides.text: Look around: trees with no leaves, scorched ground. Nothing grows here anymore. Meanwhile, on the horizon, something else lies broken.

slides.headline: A ruined city
slides.text: A city with breached walls, empty and silent. Vereshchagin knew this land: he had fought in the siege of Samarkand in 1868.

slides.headline: Tamerlane's trophy
slides.text: Its first title was The Triumph of Tamerlane, after legends of the conqueror's soldiers building pyramids from their enemies' skulls.

slides.headline: Read the frame
slides.text: But then he renamed it, and wrote on the frame: 'Dedicated to all great conquerors, past, present and to come.'

slides.headline: The painter's own war
slides.text: In 1904, Vereshchagin died aboard the battleship Petropavlovsk, sunk by mines off Port Arthur. Who would you dedicate this painting to?
